summary: Summarizes requirements of large corporate networks for the next generation of the Internet protocol suite. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Big companies explain what they need from the next Internet design.

questions: what do corporations want from ipng
why is service level agreement important
what multiprotocol support does ipng need
subtitle: Business requirements for the next-generation Internet protocol from large enterprises.

tldr.problem: Large corporations depend on networks for business-critical applications and require IPng to provide predictable service levels, smooth migration from IPv4, strong security, and support for heterogeneous network environments.
tldr.mechanism: This white paper outlines corporate requirements in four categories: smooth migration with coexistence, predictable service levels (SLAs) with quality-of-service and accounting, comprehensive security with firewall support, and accommodation of multiple protocol suites.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 was designed with these requirements in mind, incorporating quality-of-service capabilities, security extensions (IPsec), and mechanisms for traffic control and accounting.

today: RFC 1678 is an Informational document from August 1994. IPv6 design incorporated many of these corporate requirements, including quality-of-service support, security extensions via IPsec, and mechanisms for traffic control and accounting.

sections.title: Why Business Networks Matter
sections.content:
As corporations increasingly use TCP/IP for mission-critical applications like stock trading, airline reservations, and financial services, they bring business-oriented requirements to IPng design. Corporations will not connect to a network that significantly threatens the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of their data. They demand clear business advantages and an easy migration path from IPv4, otherwise there is little incentive to upgrade.

The major corporate requirements for IPng are: smooth migration from IPv4 with long-term coexistence, predictable service levels for predictable costs, security, and the ability to use multiple protocol suites. These are not technical luxuries—they determine whether corporations will adopt IPng at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies trust the Internet with their money and business secrets. They will only switch to the new Internet if it doesn't break their old stuff, costs what they expect, keeps attackers out, and works with their existing equipment.

sections.title: Migration Strategy and Coexistence
sections.content:
IPv4 has been growing for decades, so the migration to IPng will not happen quickly. IPv4 users will not upgrade unless IPng offers compelling advantages. Since new services will support both IPv4 and IPng users (as pure IPng services would exclude the majority of users), the advantage of upgrading is weak. Corporations may face decades of coexistence between the two protocols, especially if upgrading requires more resources—memory, processing, or administrative complexity—than IPv4.

IPng coexistence must be painless, not based on assumptions that IPv4 use will diminish quickly. Small, low-end systems running DOS or sub-notebooks might never be able to run IPng if it requires more memory. The CIDR address allocation scheme and careful management can extend IPv4's life, but eventually the address space exhaustion will drive migration, and corporations need confidence in a long-term upgrade path.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 will stick around for a really long time. Millions of computers might never be able to use the new Internet. The new Internet has to work alongside the old one, without making anyone buy new expensive stuff.

sections.title: Service Level Agreements and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Corporations depend on networks for business-critical applications and require predictable service levels at predictable costs. A service level agreement (SLA) is a contract specifying response times, availability percentages, throughput rates, and associated costs. IPng must enable control of networking costs and support service level management. Teleprocessing lines are expensive; in many countries, even 64 kilobit per second lines are hard to get, with lead times over six months.

IPng should support class-of-service and priority functions that let enterprises control bandwidth allocation and meet SLAs. IPv4's type-of-service field exists but has been rarely implemented; IPng should clarify whether these ad hoc techniques are adequate or whether effective new techniques must be developed. Detailed accounting is also essential: corporations want to track bandwidth usage by type (FTP versus web) and by user or department, to measure efficiency, benchmark performance, and allocate costs fairly.
sections.plainLanguage: Corporations pay for network lines and want to know they'll get the speed they paid for, for the price they negotiated. The new Internet should let them mark some traffic as important and track how much bandwidth different departments use.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
Many corporations will stick with private networks until public ones can guarantee equivalent confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data. IPng should not interfere with firewalls, which many corporations consider essential. Network security must protect not only data but also the cost-control mechanisms themselves against tampering: if an attacker can manipulate accounting or quality-of-service controls, the corporation loses both security and the ability to predict costs.

The Generic Security Service API and wider deployment of existing security technology may be sufficient to meet basic requirements. However, corporations also require policy-based filtering in firewalls: the ability to bar traffic based on source address, destination address, and transaction type. This likely requires packets to carry authenticated trace information so routers can enforce security policies without relying on manual tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies need firewalls that stop bad stuff from getting in. They also need to know that nobody can trick the network into lying about how much data was sent.

sections.title: Heterogeneity and Mobility
sections.content:
Corporate networks use multiple protocol suites due to diverse installed bases, different technical factors, and corporate decentralization. IPng must be flexible enough to accommodate major multiprotocol techniques: multiprotocol transport networking (where one protocol carries others), tunneling (both IP as tunnel and being tunneled through other protocols), and link sharing (for example, point-to-point protocol and frame relay). Different protocols have different congestion control mechanisms; fair bandwidth sharing among them is important.

Corporations are increasingly interested in wireless technology for mobile hosts. IPng should work well with wireless characteristics like delay, error rates, and variable bandwidth. Additionally, corporate topology is flexible: today, a host that moves to a different subnet needs a new IP address, which creates administrative burden. Mobile hosts and multi-tail attachment (hosts connected to multiple network paths for redundancy) require more flexible addressing models than traditional subnetting provides.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies use lots of different networking gear and systems. The new Internet should let them mix and match. Also, laptops and phones move around, and hosts sometimes need two network connections for safety.

sections.title: Configuration, Administration, and Routing
sections.content:
Corporate networks require dynamic but secure DNS updating and integration with DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol). Hosts need to update DNS records automatically when they move or when backup hosts take over for failed servers, while preventing unauthorized changes. This secure, dynamic interaction between DNS and DHCP can reduce the administrative burden of managing large networks.

Policy-based routing allows traffic to follow specific paths based on detailed source and destination information, enabling corporations to control which network lines carry traffic and to prevent free transit of other organizations' traffic. Performance under congestion is also critical: corporations need the Internet's congestion control to achieve good goodput (useful throughput) when the network is heavily loaded, measured across realistic network conditions. Finally, IPng must support continuous scaling as the Internet grows; if IPng satisfies Internet scaling requirements, it automatically satisfies corporate networks' scaling needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks need automatic ways to update the address book and set up new computers. Companies want to control which network paths their traffic uses. And the whole thing has to keep working as the Internet keeps getting bigger.
